prize_parts.citation: For establishing that biomolecular condensates form by liquid-liquid phase separation, a physical-chemical principle for organizing the interior of cells

statement.case_for: Phase separation gives cell organization a thermodynamic description: concentration, multivalency and interaction strength determine when droplets form, how they wet and age, and how they can harden into solid states. That general principle explains membraneless compartments such as P granules and nucleoli, and it now frames work on neurodegeneration and amyloid. The 2009 P-granule demonstration and the 2012 multivalent-protein experiments are concrete, replicated discoveries, and the concept has had more than fifteen years of independent confirmation. I believe it is the shortlisted candidate that most clearly introduced a new concept of molecular organisation. It is also a physical-chemical result, and physical chemistry has had little recognition relative to synthesis in recent years.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the physiological significance of condensates is still debated: it is not settled which condensates are functional in vivo and which are in vitro or overexpression artefacts, and some of the field's claims are probably overstated. Attribution is also hard. Pappu and Mittag are left out of any three-person prize, and the Medicine committee could argue the discovery belongs to cell biology. By contrast, Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is mature, unambiguous, and has near-universal impact.

responses.point: Heiner ranks phase separation first as a general thermodynamic framework and says the 2009 P-granule work is the identifiable original discovery, with Hyman and Brangwynne the cleanest pair, though omitting Rosen is a real credit question.
responses.response: I agree on the concept and the 2009 anchor. I have moved from my opening two-person view to three names, because Rosen's 2012 multivalent-protein work gave an independent in vitro demonstration and a quantitative link to valency that the P-granule observation alone did not. Since Heiner and I are both at Lund, I would like the committee to test this case against colleagues outside soft matter rather than rely on our shared view.

responses.point: Johan ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first as a game-changing, mechanistically understood method with decades of confirmation, a natural Buchwald-Hartwig pair, and a logical sequel to the 2010 prize.
responses.response: I accept the impact, the maturity and the clean two-person attribution, and I rank B052 as my first alternative. My disagreement is about novelty of concept. It is a new bond type for an established catalytic paradigm, while condensates offered a new way to think about how cells are organised. I also doubt that the Kosugi precedent is as negligible as the opening ballots imply, and I would want to see how the committee handles it before a Buchwald-Hartwig prize is called clean.

responses.point: Daniel ranks base editing first as rational chemical design with therapies already in patients, and ranks phase separation third, calling it possibly slightly early because physiological relevance is still debated.
responses.response: His maturity point is my main worry too, but I think it applies to the claims about function, not the physical phenomenon, which has been reproduced in hundreds of labs. I do not fully share his confidence about base editing. It follows the 2020 CRISPR prize, and the Target-AID priority question he raises would leave a three-person prize open to dispute. I would like to hear why he thinks the Nishida-Kondo issue is surmountable.

responses.point: Andrei ranks base editing first as a clean chemical mechanism with real therapeutic reach, and ranks PROTACs second, noting that a three-person prize leaves out credible contributors.
responses.response: I agree that the PROTAC and base-editing mechanisms are chemically clear, and that the credit problem he identifies for PROTACs is serious: a limit of three cannot cover PROTAC and molecular-glue lines. Since no PROTAC drug is approved, I think maturity makes it a weaker case than condensates today. He ranked phase separation fourth, so I would ask whether his hesitation is about the science or about attribution.

responses.point: Peter ranks long-range electron transfer through proteins first as a quantitative physical mechanism underlying respiration and photosynthesis, overdue after four decades.
responses.response: I agree this is physical chemistry of the kind I want represented, and the Gray-Winkler pair is clean. But B009 is a single-ranking candidate on the shortlist and it comes with attribution problems against Marcus, Hopfield and Dutton-Moser that he acknowledges; I find it hard to see it winning a majority. I would value hearing whether he sees it as a stand-alone prize or as a candidate to keep alive for later years.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts condensates as chemistry rather than physiology or medicine
Whether the in vivo functional role of condensates is established well enough, and whether the claims of generality are overstated
Whether three names fairly cover Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag, and where to draw the line
Whether a Buchwald-Hartwig prize would be seen as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize or as overdue
statement.conflict_note: I am at Lund with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my own research on lipid self-assembly and amyloid is close to condensate biophysics, though I do not work with any of the proposed laureates. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile; I flag the field closeness and shared institution for transparency.
